President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Right. Absolutely. Advanced logic, for example, you know, you're absolutely right. It doesn't use high energy. It really is high current and medium current. The real opportunities are in high current. That's where a lot of the sales are. I would say that, you know, the front end has an established competitor there.
Really, when we look at advanced logic, we're looking at new application in the middle of line and the end of line. Think about the kind of applications that would have been in the old back end, the metallization of, you know, for example, backside power. That's where we're looking to go, and a lot of that is material modification.
We are always looking to get very close to our customers, make sure we innovate, we can solve their valuable problems, and that's, you know, exactly what we're doing. In addition, I should point out that not only are we working with our customers on advanced logic problems, but we're also working with a very advanced institute in Europe to work out what are gonna be the next set of issues as the architectures change.
We're always looking to see an inflection point where we can take advantage of that. We've said in the past, we do have architectural differentiation in our products, and in some cases, we've been able to take really good advantage of that, like in our MUSIC technology, where that really is architectural, you know, entitlement.
Regarding memory, I think it's fair to say that the tool has been battle hardened for memory. What you see for memory is a bunch of specific applications and in many cases, what looks like dedication of species. Our tool has been optimized to really perform well under those situations. You know, basically, since it's been battle tested and fielded, high current and actually medium current, but specifically high current, we're now looking to fan that out to other customers who are in that same, you know, memory segment.
Jed Dorsheimer
Group Head of Energy and Power Technologies, William Blair
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Jack Egan of Charter Equity Research. Your line is open.
Jack Egan
Equity Research Analyst, Charter Equity Research
Great. Thanks for taking the question. I was hoping you could go over the big increase in CS&I. I mean, 17% sequential growth is pretty big for that business. You mentioned that it was stronger upgrade activity and execution on some of your service contracts. Was that strength particularly pronounced in any end market or region?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. No, I mean, honestly, it was fairly broad-based in Q4. It was, you know, multiple customers across multiple regions where we saw the strength. I think, you know, we did see people taking advantage.
We've talked a lot about how you know, as our customers start to slow down, you know, they try to find ways, they take advantage of these points to find ways to improve the efficiency and yield and throughput of their devices and to optimize the current fab space that they're utilizing.
This is, I think, the yin and the yang to you know, our business at the end of the day. We've increased the number of Purion products out into the field fairly materially over the last few years. The power of that install base is what provides us the opportunity to take advantage of these cycles, and get you know, our team goes in specifically targeting upgrades as we have them available.
We focus on making sure that our research development engineering team is working on, you know, differentiated upgrades that provide efficiencies to our customers into their fab space. You know, I think that's kind of what we were seeing here in Q4, as well as a little bit of the budgeting as we talked about before. You know, some of our fab partners and customers were, you know, looking through and working through their budget opportunities for the period.
Going into 2025, you know, we've got some, you know, relative expectations for upgrades throughout the course of the year, although we're not gonna, you know, are not currently forecasting the same level of upgrade activity in Q1 of this year, which is why we, you know, are seeing a little bit of moderation in margin. Upgrades typically provide, you know, our highest margin relative to the consolidated average, just given, you know, how valuable they can be to the customer at the end of the day.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yes. Just to kind of follow on from that, you know, this is a very focused strategy. We have been investing heavily in upgrades because it is a great opportunity for us, and the good thing about an upgrade is you get to sell it to the entire installed base. You know. Obviously, we've been making progress on contracts as well as we try to look to kind of create an annuity stream of aftermarket.
Jack Egan
Equity Research Analyst, Charter Equity Research
Great. Yeah, that's super helpful. On silicon carbide, you know, we're seeing more weakness crop up there, specifically like in the financial results of the device manufacturers. You mentioned that silicon carbide is still generally pretty resilient and that I think you said it'd only be down a bit in 2025.
With that lower EV adoption and industrial demand kind of starting to flow through the financials for that industry, could that be kind of a risk to your guidance for the H2 to be slightly better than the H1? Or is that largely contemplated in your guidance as it is today?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah, I think it's, you know, Jack, it's, you know, as we sit here today, it's expectations relative to today based on customer conversations, discussions, reviewing the current backlog, as well as, you know, some of the bookings activity we've seen through Q1, you know, so far, year to date.
You know, as Russell sort of said earlier, you know, where we sit right now, we're, you know, a little bit of an encouraging sign, probably too early to call it a victory, but encouraging signs relative to bookings where, you know, at the same point in Q4, we're ahead of our bookings rate, you know, in 2025, where we were at the same time in the Q4 timeframe. You know, as we think about silicon carbide broadly, right?
I think what we are seeing is truly diversity in the way our customers are engaging with the product, right? You know, some of them align very well with their public commentary in terms of how they're thinking about making investments, going, you know, over the course of 2025. Whereas others, you know, again, they're inconsistent, but they have a path in place to spend the CapEx dollars and build out the capacity. We see those, you know, in our expectations for 2025.
What I think helps us is, you know, we have a broad range of customers in the silicon carbide space, and we're not, you know, overly tied to one in particular customer, you know, in order for us to, you know, to meet our financial results and objectives in the course of the year. I think that is really what maybe differentiates the expectations of our performance relative to, you know, a single, you know, customer's expectations or public commentary.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
I think that's exactly right. Each customer is slightly different. You've got some that want to build ahead of demand. Some that are optimizing their yield because they wanna get into opportunities, some that are looking to gain market share, but it's difficult given the time it takes to get qualified. Some are taking the opportunity to transition to 200 mm go to 400 to 800 volt architectures, which would be trench and super junction. You know, a lot of customers are doing different things. I would say that it is very customer specific.
Jack Egan
Equity Research Analyst, Charter Equity Research
Great. That's super helpful. Thanks, guys.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Dave Duley of Steelhead Securities. Your line is open.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Yeah, thanks for taking my questions. I guess first, just a clarification. Can you help us with what silicon carbide revenue was in Q4 and for calendar 2024, dollar or percentage? Then as a follow-up-
David Ryzhik
SVP of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy, Axcelis Technologies
Hey, David, yeah, the percentage, Dave, this is Dave Ryzhik. Yeah, it should be in the slide presentation. I think we can pull that up.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
36% for the quarter and 41% for the full year for silicon carbide.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Yeah.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yep.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
6% up year-over-year.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Okay.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
That helpful, Dave?
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Yeah, very much so. Do you expect the silicon carbide business to be part of the H2 improvements? This is a follow-on to Charles's question. What exact geographic regions is silicon carbide expected to be up in the H2 of the calendar year?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. You know, geography-wise, we talked about, right, again, we're very broad-based across the board in silicon carbide, Dave. Again, we are seeing digestion. We expect China to be a lower portion of our revenue base right across the entirety of the portfolio in 2025. You know, there are strengths. There are other geographies that are having strengths in the product offer to offset some of that. We haven't given specific details on geographical expectations or anything like that.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
What we can tell you, Dave, you know, now that things, you know, customers have worked out their plans for the year, we are working very, very close with them. We are looking at bookings. We are looking at the forecast, and you know, so we do know pretty much project by project where we believe these tools are gonna go to.
You know, we've double-checked that the, you know, the fab will be ready for the tools, et cetera. You know, this is, and I'd say that, you know, we've talked about the H1 being a China digestion. We've talked about us being very broad-based on silicon carbide, and we've talked about outside of China actually, remaining, you know, relatively resilient, I'd say.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. Just, you know, again, it's, you know, broadly speaking, it's gonna be, you know, down year-over-year, but not as much as other parts of the mature book of business for us, Dave.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Other general mature is gonna be down more than, and other power stuff is gonna be down more than SiC is
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
your message.silicon carbide.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yes, that's correct.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
You talked about not wanting to break things out on geographic regions. Do you expect silicon carbide to be up in the H2 of the year, even though there's digestion in the H1?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. We're not gonna get in that level of granularity just yet, Dave.
Dave Duley
Analyst, Steelhead Securities
Okay, thanks.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Tom Diffely of D.A. Davidson & Company. Your line is open.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
Yes, good morning, and thanks for the question. Russell, I was hoping you could give us a little bit of an update on your plans to expand more into Japan, in that geographic region.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Hey, Tom. Thanks for the question, and good morning. Yes. Japan represents about $450 million in any given year. You know, our percentage of that is, as you know, sub 5%, so it's a really good opportunity for us. We've actually managed to make a bit of a beachhead there in power, and actually in some other areas as well, but like, power has been the great opportunity. Obviously the local vendors of ion implantation have often had the lion's share of the business. They haven't innovated and moved forward as quickly.
As Japan got into power, silicon, and silicon carbide, they were looking for the right equipment that you need to get into high volume, which is the whole portfolio. You can't just have a medium current machine. You need the high current and the high energy, and that's where we've been able to come in.
You know, so now we're working with those customers, working on their roadmaps and, you know, making sure that we continue to expand in those applications of power. Obviously it's not just power. I think it's interesting, you know. I think we in Q2 we mentioned we'd got a system shipping into Japan for advanced logic, so that's all shipped in Q4, and we're now in discussions for actually follow-on businesses there as well.
You know, naturally we want to build our footprint through our strongest product. As you know, once we get in with a product, we wanna fan out the applications and bring the rest of our product portfolio through with us.
You know, I think year-over-year, we're gonna see a modest improvement in revenue in Japan, and this is what I'd consider to be the seeds. You wanna get into these projects early in, where it's a mini line, and then when that mini line starts to ramp up, you wanna make sure you get the volume there. Hopefully that gives you a little bit more clarity there, Tom.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
Yeah. Is it safe to assume that both Japan and advanced logic are more of a 2026, 2027 story?
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
I think so, you know. When we built our $1.6 billion model back in the summer, we did actually have, you know, we wanna see secular growth in silicon carbide. We've talked about that. We wanna see recovery and memory in general mature. When it came to advanced logic in Japan, we had modest numbers in the model for that in 2027.
You know, you're gonna see, again, a modest improvement year-over-year building towards a modest component in our $1.6 billion dollar business. Remember, of that $1.6 billion, we're expecting, say, $400 million of that to be after market. Really, we're looking to have a very modest amount of equipment in advanced logic, where we're sowing seeds in Japan, as a component of that.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
Great. Just a quick follow-up. You know, Jamie, on the backlog side, have you seen an extension or expansion of the duration of your backlog, and has anything fallen off the backlog?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
You know, again, we see customer pushouts occur, right? These will be for, you know, purchase orders in backlog, Tom, and, you know, that was some of the activity that we saw between our Q3 call and Q4 call here was, you know, it's the customer request to push out some delivery dates and expectations. You know, not inconsistent, you know, with what, you know, our customers have said externally relative to their views on this. Yeah, and to some extent, there's a bit of a extension of the duration in the backlog as a result of that.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
Okay. Does the backlog represent the next 12 months or is it total backlog going forward?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Total backlog.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Total backlog.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
Yeah, some of it goes to the first couple of quarters.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah, exactly.
Tom Diffely
Analyst, D.A. Davidson & Company
2026. Yeah. Okay. All right, thank you.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Thanks, Tom.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Mark Miller of The Benchmark Company. Your line is open.
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Thank you for your question. I just had a question. You're projecting significantly lower sales in Q1, yet OpEx is gonna be somewhat higher. I'm just wondering if you can kind of break that down in terms of SG&A and R&D, what's going on there.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. As it relates, like, I think the general commentary is our view is to have, you know, to kind of in Q1, inherently, it's specifically gonna be relatively flat to what we saw with a slight uptick just given the seasonal component of some of the way the expenses roll through, and that impacts all the line items, you know, fairly equally across the board.
Then, you know, throughout the rest of the year, we anticipate, you know, finding ways to continue to invest in our RD&E business, and we'd expect as a percentage of sales, that number to be slightly higher than what we've had historically for that business. Sort of compensating that would be the difference would go through the SG&A line item.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. Mark, I think it's clear that, you know, we believe investing in our products and services, working close to our customers is one of the best returns we can have. You know, we actually kind of see the downturn slightly as an opportunity in the sense that our customers have more bandwidth.
We can work with them, we can develop new products, get those products qualified so then when the upturn arrives, we have new products and services to offer, and that's where we take advantage. Yeah, we are definitely, as Jamie mentioned, focused on products and services, working with our customers.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. Through this transitory cyclical digestion period, right, you know, we do expect to kind of resume growth in 2026. You know, we wanna make sure that we're positioned for that, Mark.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah.
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Okay. Basically for Q1, both SG&A and R&D is flat to slightly up. Is that correct?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yep.
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Okay. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Christian Schwab of Craig-Hallum Capital Group. Your line is open.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Great. Thanks, guys. Just in the mix of business, if we look at it by end market, you know, call it auto and industrial, is it as simple as taking silicon carbide and IGBT versus, you know, general mature to get the mix of business between, you know, end market shipments to say auto and industrial?
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Again, I didn't fully follow the question, but I would say, Christian, that basically our mature nodes are very driven by consumer, industrial, and automotive. The biggest use of silicon carbide is number one, the biggest market is automotive, but the second market that's growing actually really quite quickly is the industrial part.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah, similar dynamic.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
On IGBT as well.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Yeah.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
So if you-
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
That was my question. I'm just trying to get end market exposure. You know, in 2024, you know, what percentage of your revenue do you believe went to automotive and what percentage went to industrial/consumer applications?
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. That's not how we track it. We don't know. It's very hard for us to know what our customers ship their products into.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Correct. We don't get discrete data like that from the customers on where they're ultimately putting. We're using the same sort of, you know, general data on the utilization of silicon IGBT and silicon carbide in making those general assumptions. We don't have specific end product applications necessarily.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Great. Follow-up to that. On your automotive exposure, you know, what percentage of that do you think services the domestic Chinese market versus global players?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
On silicon carbide products we sell, right, I would say our European customers are largely the ones putting those silicon carbide devices into the automotive space today.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. I think it's fair to say that the domestic Chinese manufacturers, even the BYDs of this world, we don't believe they're qualified yet to put their devices, because of the reliability requirements, into their own electric cars. I can think of maybe one company in China that may be ahead of the curve, but ultimately, pretty much if you're gonna put silicon carbide into an electric vehicle, it's gonna come from the North Americans, Europeans, and the Japanese.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Perfect. Thank you for that clarity. Bear in mind, that's question. Go ahead.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Bear in mind, that's for the all-important MOSFET in the drive system. Remember, there's an awful lot of diodes that go into these cars as well.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
That's right.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
I think the Chinese do manufacture a large part of those components, you know, the silicon carbide diodes.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Correct. Yep. Got it. Then we talked about an investment year for customer ramps. I guess I'm kinda confused on what technology investments you're investing for. Is this, you know, for new upgrades to machines? If you could provide greater clarity of what that exactly means.
You know, is there transitions in what you're providing as far as a box structure, you know, for different applications, current energy, et cetera, you know, for 400 GV to 800 GV changing transition? I'm trying to understand the investments that you're making to drive future growth? What's changing that you're sustaining the investment?
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. You know, part of it's a little bit all of the above, right, at the end of the day. Part of it is incremental upgrade opportunities that then flow into new product development and technology. As we think about, you know, our power customers very broadly, you know, you know, our team is working through solving some of their critical challenges to improve throughput efficiency, reliability of the devices at the end of the day.
We're making investments to ensure that, you know, one, we can go back and upgrade the suite of tools that we have available for those and continue to transition our products, you know, to sort of the next generation of the technology. You know, there's examples of investments we're making, you know, in memory tools and technologies, to meet our customer roadmaps, in that space.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah. I think it's fair to say, even though we might call these like mature technologies, the equipment that goes.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yeah
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Into them are anything but. If you think about what we've been going through with silicon carbide, you know, we started off with a medium current machine, but we knew that as people moved to trenches and super junctions, they needed a high energy. In fact, the energy's actually been creeping up and up and up.
That's an example of where we have to develop the right equipment, and that's where we're putting our resources. The other thing is, I mean, we haven't talked much about it, but you know, proton implantation for IGBTs, those energies have gone up significantly, and that takes a lot of innovation to be able to support our customers, the highly productive tool that can achieve the energies.
You know, our stated strategy of, you know, driving with the secular growth in silicon carbide, making sure we, you know, have a recovery in memory and general mature, and that still takes work while actually expanding into advanced logic and Japan. All of that strategy is very well aligned with our spending on our products and services.
Jamie Coogan
EVP and CFO, Axcelis Technologies
Yep. Those are multi-year, right? Multi-year projects that, you know, we're committed to.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Great. Then my last question, you know, your implied guidance for revenue in 2025, call it $800 million plus or minus, you know, is substantially below your 2027 goal of $1.6 billion. I'm having a tough time reconciling what would have to happen in markets for that to still be an attainable objective.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Right. That was the model we provided back in July, and we showed a very kind of clear path from where we were to where we need to get to. It's fair to say that things have changed, but that was a very thoughtful model. What I would say about that model is, like, one, we're not looking to update it every quarter. But the strategy remains exactly the same.
The strategy that we've outlined doesn't change. We actually feel fairly comfortable with the 1.6. It's the timing that's a little bit uncertain. You know, obviously trying to predict the timing in the middle of a downturn when people are all kind of doom and gloom wouldn't be productive.
I think, you know, we are focused on the long-term secular growth in power, market recovery in memory, general mature, share gain in advanced logic, and geographic expansion in Japan. We believe, like I say, that'll get us to $1.6. The timing is unclear right now.
Christian Schwab
Senior Research Analyst, Craig-Hallum
Great. No, no other questions. Thank you, guys.
Operator
Thank you.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Thanks.
Operator
This concludes our question and answer session. I would like to turn it back to David Ryzhik at this time for closing remarks.
David Ryzhik
SVP of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy, Axcelis Technologies
Thank you, Didi. I want to thank everyone for joining our call and your interest in Axcelis. Didi, you can now close the call.
Operator
Thank you. This concludes the presentation. Thank you for your participation in today's conference, and you may now disconnect. Good day.

content.text:
Operator
Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Axcelis Technologies call to discuss the company's results for the Q2 2024. My name is Antoine, and I will be your coordinator for today. At this time, all participants are in listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during this session, you need to press star one one on your telephone. You would then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the presentation over to your host for today's call, David Ryzhik, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy. Please proceed.
David Ryzhik
SVP of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy, Axcelis Technologies
Thank you, operator. This is David Ryzhik, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy. With me today is Russell Low, President and CEO, and Jamie Coogan, Executive Vice President and CFO. If you have not seen a copy of our press release issued yesterday, it is available on our website. In addition, we have prepared slides accompanying today's call, and you can find those on our website as well. Playback service will also be available on our website as described in our press release. Please note that comments made today about our expectations for future revenues, profits, and other results are forward-looking statements under the SEC's safe harbor provision. These forward-looking statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to the risks inherent in our business.
These risks are described in detail in our Form 10-K annual report and other SEC filings, which we urge you to review. Our actual results may differ materially from our current expectations. We do not assume any obligation to update these forward-looking statements. Now I'll turn the call over to President and CEO, Russell Low.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Good morning, and thank you for joining us for our Q2 2024 earnings call. As you can see on slide three, we delivered strong Q2 results above our expectations, with revenue coming in at $257 million and earnings per diluted share of $1.55. Our results were driven by better-than-expected conversion of evaluation units into revenue, as well as continued robust demand for our implantation systems into the silicon carbide market. I am also pleased with how we executed on margins, which Jamie will touch on a bit later. On slide four, we show the breakdown of systems revenue by segment, which total $199 million in the quarter. Now let me touch on some key trends by market segment, starting with the mature segment on slide five, which comprised 98% of total system revenue in the quarter.
As a reminder, our mature segment represents power applications, including silicon carbide and silicon IGBTs, as well as general mature and image sensors. Within power applications, demand for EVs and hybrid EVs remain a key driver. Demand for silicon carbide applications remains strong as customers continue to expand capacity to meet the domestic production goals for the EV market. We believe we are still in the early innings of this trend. Meanwhile, demand for silicon IGBT applications remained soft in the quarter, consistent with our expectations. While EV and various forms of hybrid EVs are a key driver of our power business, we see other emerging applications requiring energy efficiency, such as power sources for data centers, which is a trend we are keeping a very close eye on, given the increased demand for power associated with artificial intelligence.
In fact, just in Q2, we've seen customers announce new silicon carbide-based trench MOSFET products targeting AI data centers, which is an attractive opportunity for Axcelis, given the high implant intensity associated with trench technology. Looking to the H2, we expect demand from silicon carbide customers to remain healthy. In general, mature in the H1, demand remained relatively consistent, but we may see some moderation in the H2. Depends on the macroeconomic environment and its impact on our customers' spending patterns. Image sensor demand has been robust in China, but has been subdued in the rest of the world due to consumer spending. We are seeing some signs of growth in this market as customer quoting activity has picked up. Turning to slide six. In advanced logic, revenue was 2% of total system revenue, yet we made significant progress in our advanced logic strategy.
We successfully closed a Purion Dragon evaluation unit that was an advanced R&D for a leading-edge application. We received a follow-on Purion H order for volume manufacturing at three nanometers, and we received an order for a Purion production unit from a new customer. As discussed at our investor event in July, the advanced logic market is an under-penetrated opportunity for Axcelis, where we are driving interest with our evaluation units and investing in R&D to solve some of the industry's growing challenges. We're in the early stages and this is a multi-year effort, but we are encouraged with the progress of our engagements and this will remain a focus for us moving forward. Moving to memory.
In line with our expectations, we did not generate any systems revenue from the market in this quarter. Ion implantation is a critical process step in the production of DRAM and NAND chips, and it's worth noting that incremental demand is expected to be driven by new wafer starts rather than technology transitions. In DRAM, given the surge in demand for High Bandwidth Memory chips for AI applications, which is absorbing DRAM capacity, we expect DRAM customers to start adding capacity as we exit 2024 and into 2025. In NAND, overall wafer front-end spending remains soft. However, we are encouraged with improving pricing and bit demand fundamentals, which needs to happen before customers invest in additional capacity. Oh, I thought you said emails. I'm like, I didn't send an email. Sorry, Mark. The evals. We currently have a number of evals underway. They're obviously in areas where we're looking to grow our business. Were you interested in the ones we have underway or the ones that we closed out in Q2, Mark?
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
The ones underway, please.
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
Okay. We do have an eval for what I'd consider to be. Well, I think we mentioned this in July. There's a tool in the field for high energy proton implantation to IGBTs. That is basically would complete our full portfolio of products for power devices with that product. Actually, that product, I think we mentioned that today, has an opportunity of about $50 million per year of additional revenue, and we're actually quite excited about that. We had a lot of inquiries about that. The other one is a silicon carbide tool in Taiwan that we're looking at. We actually started yet another eval with a large customer in Taiwan for general mature.
Last quarter, we closed an eval with this customer for general mature, and now we're doing a second eval in a different location with this customer, so we're getting kind of some traction there. As I might have already mentioned, you know, we did sign off last quarter a Purion Dragon at an advanced logic research location. We did get a Purion H200 silicon carbide tool signed off in North America for silicon carbide. There was actually a Purion H200 that was signed off in China for general mature. We continue to have quite an active funnel. Even though there's only a few going on right now because we closed so many, Mark, we are looking at the next tranche as well.
We find this is a really useful strategic tool for us to break in. There's a number of customers, whether it be, you know, additional memory customers or advanced logic, where we're looking to use the evaluations as a way to demonstrate our abilities to our customers and build that relationship.
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
When do you expect the tools currently under evaluation to be signed off on?
Russell Low
President and CEO, Axcelis Technologies
I think those will be signed off before the end of the year, I believe. The proton tool I think is imminently coming up, and also the silicon carbide tool in Taiwan is imminently coming up. I expect to have news on those in the near future. The one that we just shipped out for general mature in Taiwan, obviously that's gonna be a one-year evaluation, so that won't be until the middle of 2025 to late 2025 that we'll have any update there. You know, we do have a very high success rate with evaluations.
Mark Miller
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. I'm showing no further questions at this time. I will now turn it back over to David Ryzhik for closing remarks.
David Ryzhik
SVP of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy, Axcelis Technologies
Thank you, operator. I wanna thank everyone for joining the call. We look forward to seeing many of you at some investor conferences this quarter. With that, operator, let's close the call.
Operator
Thank you. Thank you for your participation on today's call. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.
